html:
The big picture

Every formula in this course is written in one language: a physical quantity is a numerical value times a unit, G = \{G\} \cdot [G]. A unit is only useful if everyone means the same thing by it, so units are tied to agreed standards, and every measurement is linked back to them by an unbroken chain of comparisons (traceability). The SI system supplies seven base units; since 2019 each is defined by fixing the exact value of one of seven defining constants of nature. All other units are derived units, built from the base units by multiplying and dividing with no extra factor (the SI is coherent), and prefixes scale them by powers of ten. In calculations the unit is carried through every line: converting is multiplying by factors equal to one, and checking the dimension of both sides catches wrong formulas. The type of equation you write (quantity equation, unit equation, numerical value equation, dimensional equation) decides whether it works in any units or only in the ones it was written for.

1 A quantity is a number times a unit

Lecture: board p. 1–2, slides 4–5 · Giancoli §1-4 (opening), §1-5 (opening)

Measuring a quantity means comparing it with a chosen reference of the same kind, the unit. The result is how many units fit: "18.6" alone says nothing, because 18.6 m and 18.6 mm are very different lengths. So a physical quantity is always written as a numerical value times a unit. The slides state this as

G = \{G\} \cdot [G]
Symbols
  • G — any physical quantity (a length, a mass, a force, …)
  • \{G\} — curly braces: its numerical value, a pure number
  • [G] — square brackets: its unit; read "[\ldots]" as "the unit of …"

and in words (slide 4): the unit is a particular example of the quantity, used as a reference, and the number is the ratio of the quantity to that unit. The board's example:

m = 10\ \mathrm{kg}, \qquad \{m\} = 10, \qquad [m] = \mathrm{kg}
Symbols
  • m — the mass of some body (the symbol of the quantity)
  • 10 — its numerical value; \mathrm{kg} — its unit, the kilogram

The split into number and unit depends on the unit you choose; the quantity itself doesn't. The same mass is m = 10\,000\,\mathrm{g}, with \{m\} = 10\,000 and [m] = \mathrm{g}. Later lectures use the bracket all the time: [F] = \mathrm{N}, [T] = \mathrm{s}, [f] = \mathrm{Hz}.

How to write it. The board annotates m = 10\ \mathrm{kg} with arrows: the symbol m is italic, the number is upright ("non-italic"), there is a space between number and unit, and the unit is upright. Italic marks a variable (m can be 10 kg today and 3 kg tomorrow); upright marks something fixed (the number 10, the unit kg). That is how m = 3\,\mathrm{m} can be read without confusion: an italic m is a quantity (here a length), an upright m is the unit metre. Slide 9 adds the rule behind it: quantity symbols are only recommendations (a length may be l, x, s or r), while unit symbols are fixed by the standard and printed upright.

Labelling axes

Board sketch (p. 1–2): a distance–time graph; the vertical axis is labelled s/\mathrm{m} with ticks 1–4, the horizontal axis t/\mathrm{s} with ticks 1–5. Next to the axes, boxed: "s\ [\mathrm{m}]" (p. 1) and "t\ [\mathrm{s}]" (p. 2).

The point of the sketch is the labels, not the curve. An axis carries pure numbers, so its label has to say which quantity divided by which unit gives those numbers:

\frac{t}{\mathrm{s}} = \frac{\{t\} \cdot \mathrm{s}}{\mathrm{s}} = \{t\}
Symbols
  • t — time; \mathrm{s} — the unit second
  • \{t\} — the numerical value of t in seconds

So "t/\mathrm{s}" says "the numbers on this axis are the time in seconds", and the tick 4 means t = 4\,\mathrm{s}. The same for s/\mathrm{m}: the tick 3 means s = 3\,\mathrm{m}. The same rule labels table columns.

Unclear (p. 1–2): the boxed labels

The board boxes "s\ [\mathrm{m}]" and "t\ [\mathrm{s}]" without saying what the box means. By the notation above, [t] means "the unit of t", so "t\ [\mathrm{s}]" mixes two meanings; the consistent label is "t/\mathrm{s}", which is what the axes carry. The boxes most likely mark the bracket form as common but not recommended. Which form the exam accepts isn't stated; ask in the tutorial.

Common mistake — square brackets in the textbook

Giancoli writes dimensions in square brackets: [\mathrm L] for length, [\mathrm L/\mathrm T] for a speed. In this lecture square brackets mean the unit: [v] = \mathrm{m/s}. Use the lecture's meaning in exercises and the exam; this note writes dimensions as \dim v = \mathsf L\,\mathsf T^{-1} (section 7).

2 Standards and traceability

Lecture: slide 2 · Giancoli §1-4

A unit is only useful if everyone means the same thing by it. So each unit needs a standard: a precise definition of how long one metre, or how long one second, is, chosen so that any well-equipped laboratory can reproduce it. Historically the standards were objects or natural phenomena: the metre was a platinum–iridium bar near Paris, the second a fraction of a mean solar day.

The slides ask how measurements made in different places can be compared at all:

  • Comparing every measurement directly with the same reference (the base unit) is practically not possible.

  • So the comparison runs over several steps:

    • base units are required, i.e. a measurement system;
    • every comparison adds uncertainty;
    • but all chains end at a common reference. This is traceability.
Intuition

Traceability means every measurement is linked back to the defining reference through an unbroken chain of calibrations, each with a known uncertainty. Your workshop calliper was calibrated against a gauge block, the gauge block against a national standard, and the national standard is realised from the SI definition. Each step adds a little uncertainty, but because every chain ends at the same reference, a millimetre in Klagenfurt equals a millimetre in Tokyo.

3 The SI system and its seven base units

Lecture: slides 3, 9 · Giancoli §1-4

The SI ("Système International d'Unités") was set up in 1960. Its features, as listed on slide 3:

  • a minimal set of base units, from which every other unit is built;
  • decimal prefixes (km, cm, mV, …, section 5);
  • independent names for some derived units (N, J, W, …, section 6).
FieldBase quantityTypical symbolBase unitUnit symbol
Mechanicstimetseconds
Mechanicslengthl, x, r, etc.metrem
Mechanicsmassmkilogramkg
Electrical engineeringelectric currentI, iampereA
Thermodynamicsthermodynamic temperatureTkelvinK
Chemistryamount of substancenmolemol
Opticsluminous intensityI_vcandelacd

"Minimal" means seven units are enough: every other unit is a product or quotient of these. In this course, mechanics uses only the first three (s, m, kg); kelvin and mole come with thermodynamics.

4 The SI since 2019: seven defining constants

Lecture: slides 4, 6–8, 10–12 · Giancoli §1-4

Object standards drift. The kilogram was a metal cylinder until 2019; its copies drifted against it by tens of micrograms over a century, and every mass, force and energy inherited that wobble. Since May 2019 the SI is therefore built on seven defining constants of nature instead (slides 4, 6).

How a constant can define a unit. A constant of nature also has the form number × unit. The SI now fixes the exact numerical value of each constant when expressed in SI units. Since the constant itself is postulated never to change, fixing its number fixes the unit: number × unit must equal the constant. The seven constants are chosen so that every SI unit can be written through one defining constant or through products and quotients of them (slide 6).

Defining constantSymbolNumerical valueUnit
hyperfine transition frequency of Cs-133\Delta\nu_\text{Cs}9 192 631 770Hz
speed of light in vacuumc299 792 458m s⁻¹
Planck constanth6.626 070 15 × 10⁻³⁴J s
elementary chargee1.602 176 634 × 10⁻¹⁹C
Boltzmann constantk1.380 649 × 10⁻²³J K⁻¹
Avogadro constantN_A6.022 140 76 × 10²³mol⁻¹
luminous efficacy of 540 × 10¹² Hz radiationK_\text{cd}683lm W⁻¹

The derived units in the table are related to the base units by Hz = s⁻¹, J = kg m² s⁻², C = A s, lm = cd sr and W = kg m² s⁻³ (slide 7).

Take the metre as the example. Before 1983 the metre was a thing, and c was measured. Now the number is declared exact, and the metre is whatever length makes that statement true:

c = 299\,792\,458\ \frac{\mathrm{m}}{\mathrm{s}} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad 1\,\mathrm{m} = \frac{c}{299\,792\,458} \cdot 1\,\mathrm{s}
Symbols
  • c — the speed of light in vacuum, a constant of nature (m/s)
  • m — the unit metre; s — the unit second

The step is algebra: divide both sides by 299 792 458 and multiply by s. Read the right-hand side: one metre is the distance light travels in vacuum in 1/299\,792\,458 of a second. The new definitions were chosen so that the "new" metre, second and kilogram have the same size as the old ones; nothing changes in practice.

The definitions of the base units (slides 10–12), each by fixing the numerical value of one constant:

  • second (s), time: \Delta\nu_\text{Cs}, the unperturbed ground-state hyperfine transition frequency of the caesium-133 atom, is exactly 9 192 631 770 Hz (Hz = s⁻¹).
  • metre (m), length: c is exactly 299 792 458 m s⁻¹, with the second defined via \Delta\nu_\text{Cs}.
  • ampere (A), electric current: e is exactly 1.602 176 634 × 10⁻¹⁹ C (C = A s).
  • kilogram (kg), mass: h is exactly 6.626 070 15 × 10⁻³⁴ J s (J s = kg m² s⁻¹), with metre and second defined via c and \Delta\nu_\text{Cs}.
  • kelvin (K), thermodynamic temperature: k is exactly 1.380 649 × 10⁻²³ J K⁻¹ (= kg m² s⁻² K⁻¹).
  • mole (mol), amount of substance: one mole contains exactly 6.022 140 76 × 10²³ elementary entities; this number is the fixed numerical value of N_A in mol⁻¹ and is called the Avogadro number.
  • candela (cd), luminous intensity in a given direction: K_\text{cd} for monochromatic radiation of 540 × 10¹² Hz is exactly 683 lm W⁻¹ (= cd sr W⁻¹ = cd sr kg⁻¹ m⁻² s³).

Compare also the Austrian Maß- und Eichgesetz (measurement and calibration act).

The order of the definitions matters, because each unit may only use units already defined. Solving the first four for their unit, the same algebra as for the metre:

\begin{aligned} \Delta\nu_\text{Cs} &= 9\,192\,631\,770\ \mathrm{s^{-1}} &&\Rightarrow\quad 1\,\mathrm{s} = \frac{9\,192\,631\,770}{\Delta\nu_\text{Cs}} \\ c &= 299\,792\,458\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}} &&\Rightarrow\quad 1\,\mathrm{m} = \frac{c}{299\,792\,458}\,\mathrm{s} \\ h &= 6.626\,070\,15 \cdot 10^{-34}\ \mathrm{kg\,m^2\,s^{-1}} &&\Rightarrow\quad 1\,\mathrm{kg} = \frac{h}{6.626\,070\,15 \cdot 10^{-34}}\,\frac{\mathrm{s}}{\mathrm{m^2}} \\ e &= 1.602\,176\,634 \cdot 10^{-19}\ \mathrm{A\,s} &&\Rightarrow\quad 1\,\mathrm{A} = \frac{e}{1.602\,176\,634 \cdot 10^{-19}\,\mathrm{s}} \end{aligned}
Symbols
  • \Delta\nu_\text{Cs} — frequency of the caesium-133 transition (Hz)
  • c — speed of light in vacuum (m/s); h — Planck constant (J s); e — elementary charge, the charge of one proton (C)
  • s, m, kg, A — the units being defined

Read them as:

  • second: the time in which the caesium radiation oscillates exactly 9 192 631 770 times; an atomic clock counts these oscillations.
  • metre: needs the second first, which is why the slide adds "with the second defined via \Delta\nu_\text{Cs}".
  • kilogram: the unit J s = kg m² s⁻¹ contains kg, m and s; with m and s already fixed, kg is the only unknown left, so fixing h pins it down.
  • ampere: a flow of 1/(1.602\,176\,634 \cdot 10^{-19}) \approx 6.24 \cdot 10^{18} elementary charges per second.
  • kelvin: the temperature step that changes the typical thermal energy kT by 1.380\,649 \cdot 10^{-23}\,\mathrm{J}.
Why define units through constants instead of physical objects?

An object can change (wear, absorb dirt, lose atoms) and exists in one place only; nobody can tell whether the reference or its copies are drifting. A constant of nature like h is the same everywhere and forever, and any well-equipped lab can realise the unit from it without travelling to Paris. This makes the top of every traceability chain stable and available everywhere.

5 Prefixes

Lecture: slide 13 · Giancoli §1-4

Decimal prefixes scale a unit by a power of ten, so that values stay readable: 0.000 003 m is written 3 µm.

Binary prefixes (for bits and bytes): kibi Ki = 2¹⁰, mebi Mi = 2²⁰, gibi Gi = 2³⁰, tebi Ti = 2⁴⁰, pebi Pi = 2⁵⁰, exbi Ei = 2⁶⁰, zebi Zi = 2⁷⁰, yobi Yi = 2⁸⁰.

A prefix binds to the unit (slide 13): \mathrm{mm^3} means (\mathrm{mm})^3, so the exponent applies to the prefix too:

1\,\mathrm{mm^3} = (1\,\mathrm{mm})^3 = (10^{-3}\,\mathrm{m})^3 = 10^{-3 \cdot 3}\,\mathrm{m^3} = 10^{-9}\,\mathrm{m^3}
Symbols
  • mm — millimetre, 10^{-3}\,\mathrm{m}; \mathrm{m^3} — cubic metre
  • (10^{a})^{b} = 10^{a b} — the power rule used in the third step

The same for areas: 1\,\mathrm{cm^2} = (10^{-2}\,\mathrm{m})^2 = 10^{-4}\,\mathrm{m^2}.

Common mistake — the prefix and the exponent

Tempting: 1\,\mathrm{mm^3} = 10^{-3}\,\mathrm{m^3}, because "milli is 10^{-3}". That forgets to cube the prefix: the true factor is 10^{-9}, a million times smaller. The same trap with non-metric units: one yard is 3 ft, but one square yard is 3^2 = 9\,\mathrm{ft^2}. And "1 GB" (gigabyte, 10^9 bytes) is not "1 GiB" (2^{30} \approx 1.074 \times 10^9 bytes).

6 Derived units and coherence

Lecture: slides 5, 14 · Giancoli §1-4

Every other unit is a derived unit: a product or quotient of base units. The SI is coherent: derived units are formed with no numerical factor (1 N is exactly 1 kg m s⁻², not 3.6 of something). Twenty-two derived units have special names and symbols (slide 14):

You never need to memorise the "in base units" column: each row follows from a formula you know, by substituting the units:

\begin{aligned} \mathrm{N} &= \mathrm{kg} \cdot \frac{\mathrm{m}}{\mathrm{s^2}} = \mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-2}} && \text{(force} = \text{mass} \times \text{acceleration)} \\ \mathrm{Pa} &= \frac{\mathrm{N}}{\mathrm{m^2}} = \mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-2}} \cdot \mathrm{m^{-2}} = \mathrm{kg\,m^{-1}\,s^{-2}} && \text{(pressure} = \text{force / area)} \\ \mathrm{J} &= \mathrm{N} \cdot \mathrm{m} = \mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-2}} \cdot \mathrm{m} = \mathrm{kg\,m^2\,s^{-2}} && \text{(work} = \text{force} \times \text{distance)} \\ \mathrm{W} &= \frac{\mathrm{J}}{\mathrm{s}} = \mathrm{kg\,m^2\,s^{-3}} && \text{(power} = \text{energy / time)} \\ \mathrm{C} &= \mathrm{A} \cdot \mathrm{s} && \text{(charge} = \text{current} \times \text{time)} \\ \mathrm{V} &= \frac{\mathrm{W}}{\mathrm{A}} = \mathrm{kg\,m^2\,s^{-3}\,A^{-1}} && \text{(power} = \text{voltage} \times \text{current)} \\ \Omega &= \frac{\mathrm{V}}{\mathrm{A}} = \mathrm{kg\,m^2\,s^{-3}\,A^{-2}} && \text{(Ohm's law: } R = U/I) \\ \mathrm{F} &= \frac{\mathrm{C}}{\mathrm{V}} = \frac{\mathrm{A\,s}}{\mathrm{kg\,m^2\,s^{-3}\,A^{-1}}} = \mathrm{kg^{-1}\,m^{-2}\,s^{4}\,A^{2}} && \text{(capacitance} = \text{charge / voltage)} \end{aligned}
Symbols
  • the unit symbols of the table above
  • a negative exponent means "divided by": \mathrm{s^{-2}} = 1/\mathrm{s^2}; dividing by a product flips every exponent in it, which is how the farad gets \mathrm{s^{+4}} and \mathrm{A^{+2}}

The radian and steradian are "1" because an angle is an arc length divided by a radius (m/m): the units cancel. More in 7 Rotational Kinematics and Circular Motion › 2 Measuring angles: what's a radian.

7 Accepted non-SI units and converting units

Lecture: slide 15 · Giancoli §1-5

Some non-SI units are so common that they are accepted for use with the SI (slide 15):

timeminutemin1 min = 60 s

Temperature differences may also be given in °C; absolute temperatures in K.

Converting. Every row of this table is an equation between two ways of writing the same quantity, such as 1\,\mathrm{h} = 3600\,\mathrm{s}. Dividing both sides by one of them gives a conversion factor equal to one:

1 = \frac{3600\,\mathrm{s}}{1\,\mathrm{h}} = \frac{1\,\mathrm{h}}{3600\,\mathrm{s}}
Symbols
  • h — hour; s — second; the fraction is a quantity divided by the same quantity, so it equals exactly 1

Multiplying by one changes nothing, so a quantity can be multiplied by as many such factors as needed. Choose each factor so that the unit you want to remove ends up in the denominator and cancels.

The less obvious conversions in the table follow the same way:

  • angle minute: 1' = \tfrac{1}{60}{}^\circ = \tfrac{1}{60} \cdot \tfrac{\pi}{180}\,\mathrm{rad} = \tfrac{\pi}{10\,800}\,\mathrm{rad}; one more factor \tfrac{1}{60} gives the angle second, \tfrac{\pi}{648\,000}\,\mathrm{rad};
  • hectare: hm is the hectometre, 10^2\,\mathrm{m}, so 1\,\mathrm{hm^2} = (10^2\,\mathrm{m})^2 = 10^4\,\mathrm{m^2}, a square of 100 m × 100 m;
  • litre: 1\,\mathrm{dm^3} = (10^{-1}\,\mathrm{m})^3 = 10^{-3}\,\mathrm{m^3}, and also (10\,\mathrm{cm})^3 = 10^3\,\mathrm{cm^3};
  • electronvolt: the energy one elementary charge gains through 1 V, 1.602\,176\,634 \cdot 10^{-19}\,\mathrm{C} \cdot 1\,\mathrm{V} = 1.602\,176\,634 \cdot 10^{-19}\,\mathrm{J}, since \mathrm{C} \cdot \mathrm{V} = \mathrm{A\,s} \cdot \mathrm{W/A} = \mathrm{W\,s} = \mathrm{J}.

Celsius and kelvin. The Celsius scale is the kelvin scale shifted by 273.15:

T/\mathrm{K} = \vartheta/{}^\circ\mathrm{C} + 273.15
Symbols
  • T — absolute (thermodynamic) temperature, in K
  • \vartheta — the same temperature on the Celsius scale, in °C

A shift cancels when you subtract, so a rise from 20 °C to 30 °C is 10 °C = 10 K. That is why °C is allowed for differences. A ratio or product needs the absolute temperature: 30 °C is not "1.5 times as hot" as 20 °C (303.15\,\mathrm{K} / 293.15\,\mathrm{K} \approx 1.03).

Worked example — converting a density

Steel has a density of 7.85\,\mathrm{g/cm^3}. Express it in SI base units.

  1. Write the factors equal to one that remove g and cm: \dfrac{1\,\mathrm{kg}}{1000\,\mathrm{g}} and \dfrac{100\,\mathrm{cm}}{1\,\mathrm{m}}.
  2. Use the cm factor three times, because cm is cubed: 7.85\,\dfrac{\mathrm{g}}{\mathrm{cm^3}} \cdot \dfrac{1\,\mathrm{kg}}{1000\,\mathrm{g}} \cdot \left(\dfrac{100\,\mathrm{cm}}{1\,\mathrm{m}}\right)^3.
  3. Cancel units, then multiply numbers: 7.85 \cdot \dfrac{10^6}{10^3}\,\dfrac{\mathrm{kg}}{\mathrm{m^3}} = 7850\,\mathrm{kg/m^3}.
  4. Sanity check: water is 1\,\mathrm{g/cm^3} = 1000\,\mathrm{kg/m^3}, and steel is about eight times denser. Fits.

8 Calculating with units: units in every line

Lecture: board p. 2 · Giancoli §1-5

Because a quantity is number × unit, units obey ordinary algebra: they multiply, divide and cancel like numbers. The board shows how not to do it:

F = m \cdot a = (10 \cdot 9.81) = 98.1\ \mathrm{kg\,m/s^2}

with the middle bracket and the result circled and, underneath, "Wrong!"

Symbols
  • F — force on the body (N)
  • m — mass, here 10\,\mathrm{kg}
  • a — acceleration, here 9.81\,\mathrm{m/s^2}, the gravitational acceleration g

What is being calculated is the weight of the 10 kg mass from section 1, with Newton's second law F = m\,a (properly introduced in 8 Newton's Laws and Forces). The number is right, but the line "10 \cdot 9.81" has lost its units: it no longer says what was multiplied, so nobody can check it, and the unit reappears at the end from nowhere. The rule the board makes: units go into every line. Done correctly:

\begin{aligned} F &= m \cdot a && \text{(the formula)} \\ &= 10\,\mathrm{kg} \cdot 9.81\,\frac{\mathrm{m}}{\mathrm{s^2}} && \text{(insert each quantity with its unit)} \\ &= (10 \cdot 9.81)\,\mathrm{kg} \cdot \frac{\mathrm{m}}{\mathrm{s^2}} && \text{(numbers with numbers, units with units)} \\ &= 98.1\,\mathrm{kg\,m/s^2} && \text{(multiply)} \\ &= 98.1\,\mathrm{N} && \text{(name the unit: } 1\,\mathrm{N} = 1\,\mathrm{kg\,m/s^2}) \end{aligned}

Symbols as above; N — newton, the SI unit of force.

Common mistake — units only at the end

Writing "10 \cdot 9.81 = 98.1 N" looks harmless, but it hides conversions. Had the mass been given as 10\,\mathrm{g}, the bare "10" hides that it must become 0.01\,\mathrm{kg}, and the answer would be off by a factor of 1000. Carrying units through every line turns them into a free check: if the unit at the end isn't the unit of the quantity you wanted (N for a force, m for a distance), the formula or a conversion is wrong.

Worked example — a conversion inside a calculation

A car drives at v = 54\,\mathrm{km/h} for t = 2\,\mathrm{min}. How far does it get?

  1. Convert by substituting what each unit means: 54\,\dfrac{\mathrm{km}}{\mathrm{h}} = 54 \cdot \dfrac{1000\,\mathrm{m}}{3600\,\mathrm{s}} = 15\,\mathrm{m/s}, and 2\,\mathrm{min} = 2 \cdot 60\,\mathrm{s} = 120\,\mathrm{s}.
  2. Insert with units: s = v \cdot t = 15\,\dfrac{\mathrm{m}}{\mathrm{s}} \cdot 120\,\mathrm{s}.
  3. Cancel units like numbers: \dfrac{\mathrm{m}}{\mathrm{s}} \cdot \mathrm{s} = \mathrm{m}, so s = 1800\,\mathrm{m}. The unit came out as a length, which confirms the formula has the right shape.
Problem-solving steps — converting units
  1. Write the quantity with its unit, and the unit you want.
  2. For every unit to remove, find an exact relation (1 h = 3600 s, 1 km = 1000 m) and write it as a fraction equal to one, with the unwanted unit in the denominator.
  3. For squared or cubed units, use the factor two or three times.
  4. Cancel the units first; only then multiply the numbers.
  5. Check that the remaining unit is the one you wanted, and that the size is plausible.

9 Kinds of equations and dimensional analysis

Lecture: slide 5 · Giancoli §1-7

Slide 5 sorts the equations of physics into four kinds:

Kind of equationWhat it relatesRemark on the slide
Quantity equationquantities (number × unit)independent of the unit system
Unit equationunits onlysimplification for coherent units
Numerical value equationnumbers only, valid for stated unitsfor non-coherent variables
Dimensional equationdimensions, no numbersdimension control

What the remarks mean:

  • A quantity equation like s = v\,t contains quantities with their units inside, so it is true whether you insert km and h or m and s, as long as you carry the units. All formulas in this course are quantity equations.
  • A unit equation relates only the units: [s] = [v]\,[t], i.e. \mathrm{m} = \frac{\mathrm{m}}{\mathrm{s}} \cdot \mathrm{s}. In a coherent system it contains no number; in a non-coherent mix (km/h with s) a factor like 3.6 would appear.
  • A numerical value equation contains only numbers \{\ldots\} and is valid only for the units it was written for. These appear in rules of thumb and data sheets.
  • A dimensional equation ignores numbers and even the particular unit, and keeps only the kind of quantity: length \mathsf L, time \mathsf T, mass \mathsf M, … A speed in km/h and one in m/s have the same dimension, \mathsf L\,\mathsf T^{-1}.

Dimension control. Two quantities can only be added, subtracted or set equal if they have the same dimension: metres can't be added to seconds. So both sides of a correct formula, and every term in a sum, must have the same dimension. Checking this catches many wrong formulas before any number is inserted. A dimension check can only prove a formula wrong; it cannot prove it right, because pure numbers like \tfrac12 or 2\pi have no dimension and could be missing.

Worked example — the same physics in all four forms

Distance at constant speed.

  1. Quantity equation (works in any units): s = v \cdot t. With v = 15\,\mathrm{m/s}, t = 120\,\mathrm{s}: s = 1800\,\mathrm{m}.
  2. Unit equation (check the units fit): [s] = [v]\,[t], i.e. \mathrm{m} = \frac{\mathrm{m}}{\mathrm{s}} \cdot \mathrm{s}. No factor appears, because SI is coherent.
  3. Numerical value equation (only numbers, units fixed in advance): the driving-school rule "braking distance = (\text{speed}/10)^2" means \{s\}_\mathrm{m} = \left(\{v\}_\mathrm{km/h}/10\right)^2. It only works with v in km/h and s in m: at 50 km/h it gives 25 m. Insert the same speed in m/s (13.9) and you get 1.9 m, which is nonsense.
  4. Dimensional equation (no numbers at all): \dim s = \mathsf{L} and \dim(v\,t) = \mathsf{L}\,\mathsf{T}^{-1} \cdot \mathsf{T} = \mathsf{L}. Both sides agree, so the formula can be right.
Worked example — catching a wrong formula

Someone remembers the position at constant acceleration as x = v_0 t + \tfrac12 a t. Is that possible?

  1. Dimensions of the ingredients: \dim x = \mathsf L, \dim v_0 = \mathsf L\,\mathsf T^{-1}, \dim a = \mathsf L\,\mathsf T^{-2}, \dim t = \mathsf T.
  2. Each term separately: \dim(v_0 t) = \mathsf L, but \dim(a t) = \mathsf L\,\mathsf T^{-1} (the \tfrac12 has no dimension).
  3. Verdict: the second term is a speed, not a length, so the formula is wrong. Adding one more factor t fixes the dimension: x = v_0 t + \tfrac12 a t^2, which is the correct formula from 5 Uniformly Accelerated Motion and Free Fall.
Problem-solving steps — checking a formula by dimensions
  1. Write the dimension of every quantity in the formula in terms of \mathsf L, \mathsf T, \mathsf M (look up derived units in section 6).
  2. Drop all pure numbers (\tfrac12, 2\pi, …).
  3. Work out the dimension of each term of each side separately.
  4. All terms must agree. If one doesn't, the formula is wrong; if all do, it may still be missing a numerical factor.
